title: A Bowl of Maggi in an NYC Lunchbox Became a Celebration of Indian Food Culture
excerpt: A young Indian-American girl named Aanya went viral after proudly explaining her Maggi noodles lunch in a New York City public school video celebrating AAPI Heritage Month.
body:
• A video featuring Indian-American student Aanya explaining her Maggi noodles lunch in a New York City public school went viral after being shared on the city's official social media accounts
  • The clip was part of NYC's "What's In My Lunchbox: Season Two" campaign celebrating AAPI Heritage Month through public school students' lunchboxes
  • Aanya's confident explanation of how Maggi is prepared — and her declaration that her mother's chicken curry is her favorite food — resonated deeply with South Asian viewers worldwide
  • The video sparked a broader conversation about how Indian food culture is being embraced by a new generation of diaspora children who carry their heritage into American classrooms

The Video That Launched a Thousand Comments

It started with a simple question: what's in your lunchbox? Aanya, a young Indian-American student at a New York City public school, answered with the confidence of someone who knows exactly what she's about.

"My name is Aanya, and this is what is in my lunch," she says in the video, posted on the official Instagram handle of New York City (@nycgov). "I brought Indian noodles called Maggi. We put the noodles in the pot, add hot water and our spices, and then it turns yellow."

When asked about her favorite food, she doesn't hesitate: "The chicken curry my mommy makes. She uses different spices, and they have different smells."

The clip was part of NYC's "What's In My Lunchbox: Season Two," a campaign celebrating the city's diversity and AAPI Heritage Month through public school students' lunchboxes. The city captioned the post: "True fact: there's never a curry better than mommy's."

"Growing up, I was afraid to bring in Indian food for lunch because of the rude comments people would make about it. I love how this generation is accepting."

— Social media commenter on the NYC video

Maggi: More Than Just Noodles

For anyone who grew up in an Indian household, Maggi needs no introduction. The two-minute instant noodles, manufactured by Nestlé, occupy a singular position in Indian food culture — part comfort food, part childhood ritual, part late-night survival kit. College hostels, monsoon evenings, exam nights, and Sunday afternoons: Maggi is the common denominator.

In the diaspora, Maggi carries additional weight. It is one of the first things Indian students pack when leaving for universities abroad, stuffed between winter jackets and pickle jars. For parents raising children outside India, it is one of the simplest ways to pass down a taste of home — a flavor that requires no culinary expertise, just boiling water and a yellow sachet of masala.

Aanya's matter-of-fact explanation of how the noodles turn yellow strips away the exoticism and presents Indian food as what it actually is: normal, everyday food that a kid brings to school.

A Generational Shift in the Lunchroom

The viral response to the video tells a story that goes beyond one girl's lunch. Comment sections filled with adults recounting their own childhood shame around bringing Indian food to school — the comments about the smell, the looks, the quiet decision to start asking for sandwiches instead.

That Aanya shows zero hesitation — indeed, radiates pride — suggests a generational shift. In American cities with large South Asian populations, Indian food has moved from the margins to the mainstream. Turmeric lattes sell at Whole Foods. Trader Joe's stocks paneer tikka masala. The Indian food market in the United States was valued at over $3 billion in recent years, driven by both diaspora demand and growing mainstream adoption.

NYC's decision to feature an Indian lunchbox in an official city campaign reflects this shift at the institutional level. It is not multiculturalism as performance; it is multiculturalism as census reality. New York City is home to over 300,000 Indian Americans, one of the largest concentrations in the country.

The Cultural Bridge in a Bowl

Food has always been the most accessible entry point into another culture, and for Indian families in the diaspora, it is often the last cultural practice to fade. Long after language shifts to English and festivals become abbreviated, the kitchen persists. Aanya's mother's chicken curry — made with different spices that "have different smells" — represents this continuity.

Social media users were quick to see the larger significance. "Just adorable and sweet to share the beautiful diversity of our city," wrote one viewer. Others asked Aanya's mother to share the curry recipe. A few noted that the video made them nostalgic for their own mothers' cooking.

From Shame to Pride

The trajectory from lunchbox shame to lunchbox pride tracks closely with the broader arc of South Asian visibility in American public life. Two decades ago, bringing Maggi to school was a risk. Today, a city government posts it on Instagram and calls it a "delicious ode to what makes New York special."

For the Indian diaspora watching, Aanya's video is a small thing — a child, a bowl of noodles, a 30-second clip. But it lands differently when you remember hiding your lunch under the desk.
nri_angle: The video resonated deeply with South Asian Americans who remember hiding Indian food at school, marking a generational shift toward pride in cultural food traditions.
